rationale: B wins because it treats the missing metric as the story instead of papering it over. Its "Bumble's AI relaunch will be judged on one number it hasn't reported yet" is sharper and more sellable than A's overreached "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" line, which turns one company relaunch into an unsupported category trend. A has useful bones, but one inflated angle would send the founder to the wrong inbox.
gaps_in_A: "AI matchmaking just went mainstream" and "category-standard feature, not a novelty" overclaim from one Bumble update. That is a trend piece only after outside evidence exists.

"Bumble's brand promise is that its message-first model empowers authentic connection" adds brand language the update did not supply. The real tension is women-message-first versus AI-written openers; don't decorate it.

"the relaunch is the company's public answer to the falling stock price and user decline" states intent as fact. The update says the relaunch follows those declines, not that Bumble framed it that way.

The authenticity angle asks for "any data on how many users are actually using the AI message-writing tool versus opting out" but misses the sharper disclosure/default questions: is it opt-in, and does the recipient know?
gaps_in_B: "Bumble sells subscriptions" is not in the supplied update. "Paying users" is fair; subscription-business framing needs outside confirmation.
"the first product the returned founder has put their name on" goes beyond the facts. The update says the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that nothing else came first.
The next step says "journalist-fit-check" before actual names exist. Pick the angle, build the journalist shortlist, then fit-check the people.

"one concrete decision the founder made in the relaunch that the previous leadership would not have made" asks for a counterfactual no founder can cleanly prove. Demand decision ownership and timeline instead.
